SearchSearchFacebookTwitterEmailSMSBlue SkyWhatsappPrintRedditFlipboardPinterestLinkedinLatest StoriesPoliticsU.S. NewsWorldSportsBusinessHealthSelectedTiplineMiddle East ConflictPalestinians flee and Gaza ceasefire tested as Israeli tanks cross ‘yellow line’“Israel cannot simply invoke security concerns whenever it wants to cross a boundary it agreed to respect,” one analyst said. Listen to this article with a free profile00:0000:00A young Palestinian pushes a wheelchair carrying children as residents evacuate their homes and tent shelters in Nuseirat, in the central Gaza Strip, following an Israeli army order to leave the area.Eyad Baba / AFP via GettyShareAdd NBC News to GoogleNov. 19, 2026, 10:58 AM ESTBy Chantal Da SilvaIsrael’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday.

As tanks rolled into central Gaza on Wednesday, residents could be seen carrying blankets and other belongings away from their tents in pictures and video taken shortly after the Israeli military began what it said was an operation targeting a “terror tunnel.”

Others could be seen rolling away mattresses on carts and pushing loved ones in wheelchairs away from the scene near the Nuseirat camp in central Gaza. At least one person was reported to have been killed in an Israeli airstrike near the raid, Palestinian medics said, according to Reuters.

“Bullets were fired at us,” Amna al-Gasar, 49, told NBC News after she fled the scene with her young children, her baby in a pink fluffy sweater strapped to her chest. She said her family had received “evacuation orders” from the Israeli military and that tanks had advanced on the area.

Families in Gaza live surrounded by rubble and toxic waste02:06“This is the 14th time that we’re getting displaced,” al-Gasar said, who added that she is from Gaza City in the north of the enclave which is now on the side of the “yellow line” occupied by Israeli forces. “Where should we go? We are exhausted. This is not a life,” she said.

Muna Abu Shehadeh, 37, said in a separate interview that along with some of her relatives, she left “with nothing but our children — no bedding, no food, and no water.” She added that she had a daughter who was ill, as well as a baby, and that they had to leave behind what few supplies they had.

The Israeli military told NBC News the ground operation was the first to be executed beyond the yellow line — the boundary marking the roughly 60% of Gaza that remains occupied by Israeli forces — since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire with Hamas came into effect in October 2025.

Separately, in a joint statement with the Israel Security Agency, or Shin Bet, the Israel Defense Forces said the operation was a “targeted” assault aimed at dismantling a tunnel that “posed an immediate and direct threat” to troops.

An 11-year-old Palestinian boy at Nasser Hospital, after sustaining injuries during an Israeli attack in Khan Younis on Thursday.Abed Rahim Khatib / Anadolu via GettyThey said a warning had been issued to civilians in the area prior to the operation, though they did not expand on how exactly warnings were issued and whether they expanded beyond an announcement published online, when asked by NBC News.

Israeli forces would continue to operate to “remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts” by Hamas to harm Israeli civilians or troops, the statement added.

A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Thursday that the operation west of the yellow line had “ended,” though they could not confirm when exactly the offensive came to a close. Hamas condemned the ground operation, calling it a violation of the ceasefire agreement.

“Israel agreed to withdraw to the ‘yellow line,’ which was supposed to establish a mutually understood boundary until further withdrawals could be negotiated,” he said Thursday. Sending ground forces a few hundred feet beyond that line and “forcing civilians to flee undermines the agreement,” he added.

“Israel cannot simply invoke security concerns whenever it wants to cross a boundary it agreed to respect,” he said, adding that its assertion of a threat had “not been independently substantiated.” The operation risked undermining “any meaning” the yellow line has held as a boundary under the ceasefire agreement, he said.

The Israeli government and military did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the accusation that the ceasefire agreement had been violated.

The truce has already been marked by regular Israeli strikes, with more than 1,600 people killed in the enclave since the truce began, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the territory. Israel says at least five soldiers have been killed within the same amount of time, according to Reuters.

Both Israel and Hamas have repeatedly traded accusations of ceasefire violations.

“Israel has been violating the ceasefire pretty periodically since it came into place, so it’s nothing new on that front,” Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in defense studies at King’s College London, said Thursday of the Israeli military’s ground operation.

“It’s the scale of the violation,” he said, adding the ground assault and use of tanks signifying an “escalation” from Israel.

Palestinians living in the al-Dawa neighborhood north of Nuseirat refugee camp flee their homes Wednesday.Hassan Jedi / Anadolu via GettyBoth Pinfold and Krieg noted that the ground operation comes at a time of great political uncertainty for Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces losing his prime ministership after elections last month.

While Netanyahu’s Likud party gained the most votes, President Isaac Herzog tasked his main rival, Gadi Eiskenot, with forming a coalition government based on the premise that he was most likely to succeed in doing so.

Netanyahu has railed against the possibility of Israel’s Arab-led parties joining a coalition and both Pinfold and Krieg suggested that he might be seeking to ramp up pressure around  security concerns.

Pinfold said Netanyahu was also likely “trying to see how far he can go on the Gaza front,” particularly as the U.S. continues to sideline Israeli involvement in the war with Iran.

“I suspect Israel is testing how far it can push the Americans without provoking a serious response,” Krieg said. Israel could also be seeking to “establish a precedent for what amounts to a permanent right of hot pursuit” in Gaza, even beyond its current “yellow line” and even into the future as efforts to advance the peace continue to stall, he added.

A campaign billboard featuring Netanyahu and Eisenkot, in Tel Aviv before the Israeli elections in October.David Goldman / AP Photo/David GoldmanElsewhere, President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, the body that is overseeing the execution of the U.S.-brokered ceasefire, delivered a bleak report Tuesday on its progress to the United Nations Security Council, warning that the fragile deal was in danger of collapse, Reuters reported.

The board said both Israel and Hamas should uphold the commitments made in the agreement, according to Reuters, which obtained a copy of the report. But Hamas’ disarmament and the militant group’s calls for the Israeli military’s withdrawal from Gaza have proven major sticking points in efforts to propel the deal forward.

Fleeing from the area of Israel’s ground operation Wednesday, al-Gasar said Palestinians “need a solution.”

“All we ask for is safety and security. We’re not asking for a lot,” she said. “All of this talk in the media about advancement in negotiations, but instead we find advancement of tanks.”
